hints: Focus on the attacking species in each reaction, is $\text{CN}^-$ electron rich or electron poor?
In $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$, $\text{Br}$ is replaced by $\text{CN}$, while in $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ the $\text{C=O}$ double bond becomes single.
Link replacement to substitution and gain across a double bond to addition, then decide if an electron rich attacker means nucleophilic.
walkthrough:
**Analyse the first reaction**

Think like the $\text{CN}^-$ ion. It has a lone pair and a negative charge, so it is a nucleophile that loves positive carbon.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CN} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Name the first mechanism**

The $\text{C-Br}$ bond is polar, so carbon is slightly positive. $\text{CN}^-$ attacks it and pushes out $\text{Br}^-$ as a leaving group.

One group is swapped for another, so this is nucleophilic substitution.

**Analyse the second reaction**

Now look at propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$. The $\text{C=O}$ bond is very polar, with carbon $\delta+$ and oxygen $\delta-$.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_3$$

**Name the second mechanism**

The nucleophile $\text{CN}^-$ attacks the $\delta+$ carbonyl carbon. The pi bond breaks and then $\text{H}^+$ adds to oxygen to form a cyanohydrin.

Two groups add across a double bond, so this is nucleophilic addition. Together we get nucleophilic substitution then nucleophilic addition.

options.A: Incorrect. Neither reaction is electrophilic. An electrophile accepts electrons, but here $\text{CN}^-$ donates electrons, so it is a nucleophile in both cases.
options.B: Incorrect. The second half is right, but the first half is wrong. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{KCN}$ is not electrophilic substitution, halogenoalkanes undergo attack by nucleophiles, not electrophiles.
options.C: Incorrect. The first half is right, but the second half is wrong. Addition to a carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ by $\text{CN}^-$ is started by a nucleophile, not an electrophile.
options.D: Correct. $\text{CN}^-$ replaces $\text{Br}$ in the halogenoalkane by nucleophilic substitution, and $\text{CN}^-$ adds across the $\text{C=O}$ in the ketone by nucleophilic addition to give a cyanohydrin.
